# 2025 Enderlin tornado
The 2025 Enderlin tornado was a large and violent tornado that struck rural areas near Enderlin, North Dakota, on June 20, 2025. Rated an EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, it was the first tornado to receive the EF5 classification in the United States in over 12 years. The tornado reached an estimated peak wind speed of 210 mph (338 km/h) and grew up to 1.05 miles (1.7 km) wide at its largest point. Over a 19-minute lifespan, it carved a path of destruction approximately 12 miles (19 km) long across portions of Ransom and Cass counties in southeastern North Dakota. The tornado destroyed multiple farmsteads, derailed a freight train, and caused three fatalities, making it one of the deadliest tornadoes in North Dakota in decades. Its occurrence ended a long period with no EF5 tornadoes nationwide and marked only the third F5/EF5 tornado on record in North Dakota’s history.
## Meteorological background
In mid-June 2025, a widespread severe weather outbreak impacted the northern Great Plains. On June 20, an intense mesoscale convective system developed over the region, producing a long-lived derecho (a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms) that swept eastward across North Dakota and beyond. This system generated destructive straight-line winds of 70–106 mph and spawned numerous tornadoes along its path. In eastern North Dakota alone, at least nine tornadoes were reported that evening amid the severe thunderstorms. The atmosphere was characterized by very warm, moist air and strong wind shear, providing an environment conducive to tornadic supercells forming ahead of the main derecho squall line.
One particularly strong supercell developed over Ransom County in southeastern North Dakota on the night of June 20. Around 11:00 p.m. local time, this storm produced the tornado near the small city of Enderlin, about 60 mi southwest of Fargo. The tornado touched down south of Enderlin at approximately 11:02 p.m. CDT and tracked toward the north-northeast. It moved through mainly rural farmland and open country, eventually crossing the Maple River and the Ransom–Cass county line. The tornado remained on the ground for roughly 19 minutes before dissipating around 11:21 p.m. CDT in southwestern Cass County. Its formation occurred after dark, making it a rain-wrapped, nighttime tornado that was difficult to see, which added to the danger for anyone in its path.
## Tornado event and damage
Damage to a farm property east of Enderlin in the aftermath of the June 20, 2025 tornado. The violent tornado destroyed several farms, obliterated buildings, and tossed heavy machinery and vehicles, indicating extreme wind speeds.
As it intensified, the Enderlin tornado grew to a massive size—over one mile wide at peak—and inflicted devastating damage in a mainly rural area east of Enderlin. Entire farmsteads were leveled: at least two farm homes were completely destroyed and several outbuildings and grain bins were obliterated. In one case, a farmhouse was swept entirely off its foundation, leaving only the basement behind, a level of destruction consistent with the highest tornado intensity. Sturdy trees in the tornado’s path were debarked and reduced to bare trunks, and crop fields were scoured by the intense winds. A free-standing communications tower collapsed, and high-voltage transmission towers were also blown down by the tornado.
One of the most striking incidents occurred south of Enderlin, where the tornado struck a moving freight train. The powerful winds derailed 33 rail cars, including 19 fully loaded grain hopper cars and 14 tanker cars. Several of these heavy rail cars were violently thrown from the tracks—one empty tanker car was lofted and flung about 500–600 feet from the rail line into a field. This extraordinary feat of tossing large, weighty objects indicated the presence of winds well over 200 mph at that location. Engineers later estimated that roughly 230 mph winds would be required to hurl a 72-ton grain hopper car the way the Enderlin tornado did. The mangled train cars, along with the wiped-out buildings and shredded trees, served as key evidence of the tornado’s extreme intensity.
Despite its ferocity, the tornado narrowly missed the town of Enderlin itself. The city of Enderlin experienced mainly peripheral effects, such as downed power lines and power outages, but the populated town center was largely spared from major damage. However, rural residents in the direct path suffered catastrophic impacts. The tornado claimed three lives in two separate farm locations east of Enderlin. At one farm, an elderly husband and wife were killed when their home was obliterated, and at another nearby farm a third person was killed as the tornado destroyed that residence as well. All three victims were aged in their 70s or 80s. No other serious injuries were reported, in part because of the sparse population in the tornado’s immediate path and the fact that few vehicles were on rural roads at that late hour. The three fatalities made this the deadliest North Dakota tornado in nearly five decades – no tornado in the state had killed three or more people since an F4 tornado in 1978 that caused five deaths in Elgin, North Dakota.
## Aftermath and emergency response
In the hours and days following the disaster, local and state authorities mobilized to respond. First responders from Enderlin and surrounding communities, along with sheriff’s deputies, conducted search-and-rescue operations and welfare checks through the night of June 20–21. They faced hazardous conditions immediately after the tornado, as lightning, heavy rain, and high winds from the broader storm system continued in the area, complicating the response efforts. By daybreak on June 21, the scope of the damage was evident with debris from homes and farms strewn across fields and roads. Emergency crews and utility companies worked to clear roadways and restore electricity to Enderlin and nearby rural areas that had lost power.
North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster emergency on June 21, 2025, in the wake of the tornado and the accompanying severe storms. This declaration activated the state’s emergency operations plan and made state resources available to support the affected communities. “Our hearts and sympathies go out to the family and friends of the three North Dakotans who tragically lost their lives in Friday’s tornado, and to the close-knit community in Enderlin, which suffered widespread damage,” Governor Armstrong stated in announcing the disaster declaration. He also commended the swift actions of first responders and local officials in the aftermath of the storm.
In the weeks that followed, community and volunteer efforts played a significant role in the recovery. Hundreds of volunteers from Enderlin and neighboring counties turned out to help farmers and residents clean up debris scattered across fields and properties. Relief organizations and local groups organized cleanup crews, and even drones were used to help locate and collect pieces of wreckage and personal belongings thrown by the tornado. Local banks and charities established relief funds to assist families who lost homes or farm buildings, and mental health services were offered to survivors coping with trauma. One such effort, the Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund set up at a regional bank, provided financial assistance to those hardest hit. Community leaders noted that some residents faced unexpected rebuilding costs due to insurance gaps, underscoring the need for continued financial support during recovery.
At the state level, damage assessments were conducted throughout the summer to quantify the destruction from the tornado and the wider storm outbreak. On July 21, Governor Armstrong formally requested a federal disaster declaration to unlock additional recovery funds for North Dakota. The President of the United States approved the disaster declaration in early September 2025, making federal aid and FEMA assistance available to supplement state and local recovery efforts. This assistance helped fund the rebuilding of infrastructure and provided grants to individuals and businesses who suffered uninsured losses. Governor Armstrong welcomed the federal support, calling the storm “one of the most powerful summer storms in recent history” for the state and emphasizing the importance of disaster aid in helping communities rebuild. By late 2025, reconstruction of damaged farms was under way, and the Enderlin area continued its long-term recovery from the historic tornado.
## Analysis, rating, and historical significance
Because of the extraordinary damage caused by the Enderlin tornado, meteorologists took an unusually long time to analyze and rate its intensity. Initially, the National Weather Service (NWS) office in Grand Forks rated the tornado as an EF3 based on the damage observed in the immediate aftermath. This preliminary rating (indicative of winds around 140 mph) was assigned partly because many of the structures hit were not engineered buildings, and standard damage indicators were limited in such rural areas. However, the scope of destruction clearly suggested a very powerful tornado, so the NWS launched an in-depth investigation into the event. In the weeks after the tornado, experts from the NWS collaborated with wind engineers and researchers – including members of the Northern Tornadoes Project in Canada and renowned storm damage experts like Tim Marshall and Dr. Greg Kopp – to perform a forensic analysis of the damage. They examined high-resolution aerial imagery, surveyed structural debris, and performed calculations on the derailed train cars and other unique damage indicators. The team also reviewed radar data, which showed extremely intense velocity signatures co-located with the time and location of the most severe damage.
This comprehensive re-analysis concluded that the tornado’s winds had exceeded 200 mph. On October 6, 2025, the National Weather Service announced that the Enderlin tornado’s rating was being upgraded to EF5, the highest category on the Enhanced Fujita scale. The revised damage survey determined that wind speeds “greater than 210 mph” occurred at the site of the train derailment and other locations, warranting the EF5 classification. In their report, meteorologists noted classic EF5 indicators such as a clean-swept foundation of a house and trees stripped completely of bark and branches. The tossed railroad cars – an unconventional damage indicator – provided additional, crucial evidence. According to the analysis, the distances and weights involved (rail cars up to ~130 metric tons thrown hundreds of feet) implied wind forces in the EF5 range. The upgrade made the Enderlin tornado the first EF5 tornado in the United States since May 2013, ending what had been the longest period on record without any tornado rated EF5 in the country. The 12-year “EF5 drought” was notable, as several strong tornadoes in the intervening years had come close but did not meet the criteria due to lack of suitable damage evidence.
The 2025 Enderlin tornado holds significant places in weather record books. It became one of only three tornadoes ever documented at F5 or EF5 intensity in North Dakota. The other two were historic events in the 1950s: an F5 tornado in Fort Rice, ND in 1953, and the devastating Fargo tornado of June 20, 1957, which was also rated F5 and killed 12 people in the Fargo area. Thus, the Enderlin tornado was North Dakota’s first tornado rated in the top category in 68 years. With three fatalities, it was also the state’s deadliest tornado in nearly 47 years, the worst since the July 1978 F4 tornado in Elgin, ND that caused five deaths. Nationally, the confirmation of an EF5 broke a long absence of such top-end events and reminded meteorologists and the public that even the northern Plains are capable of producing tornadoes of the maximum destructive intensity. The Enderlin tornado of June 20, 2025 will be remembered not only for its tragic impacts on a small community, but also for its historic intensity and the extensive scientific effort that went into understanding the full magnitude of its force.

National Weather Service upgrades tornado to EF5, the first in 12 years
=======================================================================

This video shows the EF5 tornado in North Dakota. (Source: KVRR via CNN Newsource)

By [The Associated Press](https://www.kbtx.com/authors/associated-press/)

Published: Oct. 6, 2025 at 1:33 PM CDT|Updated: Oct. 6, 2025 at 5:01 PM CDT

ENDERLIN, N.D. (AP) - A deadly [tornado](https://apnews.com/article/north-dakota-tornado-deaths-08d9ce8cbea78a8b86d6a66040723814) that tore across southeastern North Dakota this summer has been upgraded to an EF5 with winds topping 200 mph (322 kph), the strongest classification of tornado and the first confirmed on American soil in a dozen years, meteorologists said Monday.

The June 20 twister near the town of Enderlin killed three people and at its largest was 1.05 miles wide (1.7 kilometers), carving a path across the prairie for just over 12 miles (19 kilometers). Meteorologists from the National Weather Service office in Grand Forks estimated the tornado’s winds reached 210 mph (338 kph), according to the newly released analysis.

![Image 1: This photo shows the EF5 tornado in North Dakota.](https://gray-kbtx-prod.gtv-cdn.com/resizer/v2/T336WDUT2RDFPGZWTZ6LQBSUJI.png?auth=18ef673cdc24f289e7f8b6936ff9cfa31d9ccb016d20dddd7e28b2c6e953edd8&width=980&height=546&smart=true)

This photo shows the EF5 tornado in North Dakota.(KVRR via CNN Newsource)

The 1999 Bridge Creek-Moore tornado in Oklahoma holds the record of the strongest winds ever recorded in the U.S. at 321 mph (517 kph).

Since the National Weather Service began using Enhanced Fujita scale in 2007, there have been 10 tornadoes categorized as EF5. The 12-year gap between top-of-the-scale ratings is the longest since the agency started keeping records in 1950. The earlier tornadoes were assessed using an older version of the EF scale called the Fujita scale.

“In the last kind of 12 years, there’s been several strong tornadoes that have come close, but there haven’t been known damage indicators at that time to support the EF5 rating,” said Melinda Beerends, meteorologist in charge at the National Weather Service in Grand Forks.

“It’s hard sometimes to get tornadoes to hit something,” she said.

The morning after the EF5 tornado, meteorologists from the Grand Forks office headed into the field to assess the damage. They studied how the twister had uprooted trees, tipped over fully loaded rail cars, toppled transmission towers and destroyed farmsteads, including one that had its foundation swept clean with just the basement remaining.

“The city of Enderlin, other than losing power, pretty much went unscathed,” said Mayor Deon Maasjo. Two men and a woman were killed at two locations east of the town, which is about 40 miles (65 kilometers) southwest of Fargo.

Determining a tornado’s strength usually takes days or weeks, as meteorologists study the damage to buildings and trees. This case took much longer because of the unusual damage to rail cars, including one that was picked up and hurled far from the rest. The meteorologists worked with engineers and wind damage experts to conduct additional surveys and forensic analysis to determine the EF5 rating, up from the initial estimate of EF3.

The tornado was caused by warm, moist air in a place that’s ripe for a thunderstorm, Beerends said. But there was also a high amount of wind shear, which is a variation of wind speed and direction that created the conditions for the tornado.

In recent years, tornadoes have been occurring with greater frequency [east](https://apnews.com/article/9ddb3deeec9a49d6a1349b78f1ca0f03) of the Mississippi River, said Victor Gensini, professor of atmospheric sciences at Northern Illinois University.

“If you look 40 to 50 years ago, the tornadoes that were happening in places like Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas are kind of happening there with less frequency, and we’re seeing more tornadoes in places like Birmingham, Little Rock and Memphis,” he said.

Though meteorologists aren’t sure what’s causing the trend, the higher frequency of tornadoes in the Mid-South and Midwest is notable because it’s closer to population centers, Gensini said, so there’s a greater chance a tornado may hit something.

The last recorded EF5 [tornado](https://apnews.com/general-news-779e55edec9f466581043606bfd5f8ea) was on May 20, 2013, in a town outside Oklahoma City, killing 24 people and injuring more than 200 others. That tornado tore through hundreds of homes, a school, hospital and bowling alley in Moore, where nearly a decade later, droves of [moviegoers](https://apnews.com/article/twisters-movie-oklahoma-tornadoes-moore-d053e74f86761511a6b1615b17abee88) lined up to watch the 2024 film “Twisters.”

ENDERLIN, N.D. — A [tornado](https://www.inforum.com/news/three-killed-as-tornado-strikes-cass-county-overnight) that killed three people this summer in southeast North Dakota has been reclassified EF5, the most damaging level for a twister.

The June 20 tornado that destroyed at least two homes, damaged other buildings and derailed a train near Enderlin reached speeds that exceeded 210 mph, the National Weather Service announced Monday, Oct. 6. The minimum speed for an EF5 tornado is 201 mph.

ADVERTISEMENT

"It is a significant part of North Dakota history, being one of three tornadoes now officially being rated as F5 or EF5," said Tyler Thomas, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Forks.

EF5 is the highest rating for a tornado on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Until 2007, meteorologists used the Fujita Scale to classify tornadoes.

[Enderlin tornado](https://www.scribd.com/document/929054510/Enderlin-tornado#from_embed "View Enderlin tornado on Scribd") by [April Baumgarten](https://www.scribd.com/user/682740467/April-Baumgarten#from_embed "View April Baumgarten's profile on Scribd")

Meteorologist Ted Fujita introduced the Fujita Scale in 1971 after studying damage caused by the [1957 tornado](https://www.inforum.com/newsmd/60-years-later-fargos-1957-tornado-still-haunts) that hit Fargo. That 700-foot wide tornado killed 12 people and injured at least 100 others as it traveled 9 miles, according to the Weather Service.

"The Fargo F5 back in 1957 was actually the first F5 ever rated by Ted Fujita," Thomas said.

The other North Dakota tornado to receive an F5 ranking was a 1953 twister that hit Fort Rice, about 20 miles south of Bismarck. That tornado hit between 260 and 318 mph and was 1,800 feet wide, the weather service said.

The small town was mostly destroyed, with the tornado killing two people and injuring 20, the Weather Service said.

The last EF5 tornado in the U.S. was recorded in 2013 in Moore, Oklahoma.

ADVERTISEMENT

The June tornado near Enderlin was initially classified as EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale and was one of multiple tornadoes that storms produced in the region that day.

  ![Image 5: 062125.N.FF.tornado10.jpg](https://cdn.forumcomm.com/dims4/default/f918a1e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5679x3786+0+0/resize/840x560!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fforum-communications-production-web.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F3d%2F412f8e874e3e80cf3436e4b5e947%2F062125-n-ff-tornado10.jpg)

Residents of a home about a mile east of Enderlin, North Dakota, assess damage to their property on Saturday, June 21, 2025, following a tornado that struck late Friday evening, killing three people, and causing widespread damage in the region.

Anna Paige / Forum file photo

The Enderlin tornado started south of the city and traveled northeast 12 miles, the Weather Service said. It stretched to slightly over a mile wide, destroying crops and buildings in its path, according to the National Weather Service.

The tornado killed Michael and Katherine Dehn, both 73, at their home about a mile east of Enderlin on Highway 46, the Cass County Sheriff’s Office said. It also took the life of 89-year-old [Macario Lucio,](https://www.inforum.com/community/debris-from-enderlin-tornado-victims-lands-in-two-moorhead-yards) authorities said.

No injuries were reported.

The weather service conducted additional survey work to determine whether to reclassify the tornado. The derailed train played a key role in updating the tornado's rating, Thomas said. Inspections revealed the tornado tipped over several fully-loaded grain cars and lofted tanker cars, including an empty one blown about 475 feet away from the tracks, the weather service said.

"We consulted with experts around the field," Thomas said.

ADVERTISEMENT

"Thus, we did the research and worked with those experts to determine what that rating would be," he said.

Surveyors also noticed the tornado left stumps where trees once stood, the Weather Service said. Some trees were torn out of the ground completely, revealing "root ball displacements," the weather service said.

In one instance, surveyors couldn't determine the original location of the displaced tree, the weather service said.

A line of cars stacks up on 140th Avenue Southeast, one mile east of Enderlin, North Dakota, on Saturday, June 21, 2025, as residents check on one another following a tornado that struck late Friday evening, killing three people. Wind gusts in excess of 75 miles per hour caused widespread damage in the region.

Anna Paige / Forum file photo

Other trees showed signs of debarking in a "sandpapering" effect, which correlates with stronger, rarer tornadoes, Thomas said.

After looking at the damage caused by the Enderlin tornado, experts determined evidence supported a higher ranking, he said. The Enderlin tornado is the first EF5 tornado recorded in North Dakota since the National Weather Service started using the Enhance Fujita Scale in 2007, Thomas confirmed.

The U.S. has documented 60 F5 or EF5 tornadoes since 1950, Thomas said. Enderlin's is the 10th EF5 reported since the scale change.

Enderlin is about 55 miles southwest of Fargo.

Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster on Saturday.

At least three people were killed in North Dakota after severe weather swept across the region overnight, authorities said.

The Cass County Sheriff's Office said it was dispatched to rural Enderlin, North Dakota, for tornado damage at a residence at approximately 11:40 p.m. local time on Friday night.

Once deputies arrived on the scene, the Enderlin Fire Department let them know that storm chasers had located two deceased people as a result of the tornado, according to a statement from the sheriff's office.

![Image 1](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/f7328f18-cb50-4df6-aa60-e17b576e561e/cass-county-presser-ht-jt-250621_1750525949482_hpMain_16x9.jpg)

Cass County Sheriff Jesse Jahner speaks at a press conference in Cass County, North Dakota, June 21, 2025.

WDAY

"Shortly after learning of this, the Enderlin Fire Department was dispatched to another location, and a third deceased person was found as a result of the tornado," officials said. "Deputies found extensive damage to the area and began conducting well-being checks on people with several partner agencies."

![Image 2](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/2bea006c-776b-4c7f-ac1b-b5f84dfc5a51/north-dakota-storm-damage-ht-jt-250621_1750525804906_hpMain_16x9.jpg)

In this screen grab from a video, storm damage is shown in Cass County, North Dakota on June 21, 2025.

WDAY

Law enforcement, the Enderlin Fire Department, and other first responders will continue searching the area and checking on residents, the sheriff's department said.

"The storm was still active when they responded, and was very dangerous," Cass County Sheriff Jesse Jahner told reporters Saturday, according to ABC affiliate WDAY in Fargo, North Dakota. "And to come across the scene ... people that they're familiar with is a difficult situation."

Popular Reads
-------------

North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Saturday declared a statewide disaster and activated the State Emergency Operations Plan after multiple tornadoes, strong winds and hail caused widespread damage Friday across North Dakota.

"Our hearts and sympathies go out to the family and friends of the three North Dakotans who tragically lost their lives in Friday's tornado, and to the close-knit community in Enderlin, which suffered widespread damage," Armstrong said. "We thank our dedicated first responders and community leaders, including our many volunteer first responders, for their swift action to keep residents safe and help them recover."

The State Emergency Operations Plan directs all state agencies to utilize their response and recovery resources accordingly, as well as coordinate with the appropriate federal agencies to help local and tribal officials restore services and infrastructure.

A long-lived destructive thunderstorm event, known as a "derecho" had slammed an area more than 300 miles long with wind gusts between 70 and up to 106 mph.

Nine tornadoes were reported with these strong thunderstorms in eastern North Dakota, and greater than baseball-sized hail was also seen from eastern Montana to northwestern Minnesota.

Heavy rain from the storm complex also produced spotty flash flooding, which prompted multiple water rescues in Fargo.

Enderlin tornado that claimed 3 lives is North Dakota’s deadliest since 1978
============================================================================

###### By: [Mary Steurer](https://northdakotamonitor.com/author/mary-steurer/ "Posts by Mary Steurer") \- June 24, 2025 5:00 am

[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Enderlin%20tornado%20that%20claimed%203%20lives%20is%20North%20Dakota%E2%80%99s%20deadliest%20since%201978%20https%3A%2F%2Fnorthdakotamonitor.com%2Fbriefs%2Fenderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?text=Enderlin%20tornado%20that%20claimed%203%20lives%20is%20North%20Dakota%E2%80%99s%20deadliest%20since%201978&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnorthdakotamonitor.com%2Fbriefs%2Fenderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978%2F&via=)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnorthdakotamonitor.com%2Fbriefs%2Fenderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978%2F)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnorthdakotamonitor.com%2Fbriefs%2Fenderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978%2F&title=Enderlin%20tornado%20that%20claimed%203%20lives%20is%20North%20Dakota%E2%80%99s%20deadliest%20since%201978)[](mailto:?subject=Enderlin%20tornado%20that%20claimed%203%20lives%20is%20North%20Dakota%E2%80%99s%20deadliest%20since%201978&body=https://northdakotamonitor.com/briefs/enderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978/)

[![Image 3](https://northdakotamonitor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Storm_pix_04-scaled.jpg)](https://northdakotamonitor.com/briefs/enderlin-tornado-that-claimed-3-lives-is-north-dakotas-deadliest-since-1978/)

A tornado on June 20, 2025, blew the roof off this home about 3 miles east of Enderlin, N.D. The storm claimed three lives, making it the deadliest tornado to hit North Dakota since 1978. (Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)

The weekend tornado that killed three people in rural Enderlin was the most deadly North Dakota has seen in nearly five decades.

While North Dakota sees an average of [about 23 tornadoes](https://www.weather.gov/media/bis/North_Dakota_Tornado_Details.pdf) a year, fatalities are rare, [National Weather Service data indicates.](https://www.weather.gov/media/bis/North_Dakota_County_Statistics.pdf) The last tornado to claim three or more lives in the state was a July 4, 1978, storm that killed five people in Elgin. It was recorded as an F4.

Between the 1978 tornado and last weekend’s storm, North Dakota recorded four fatal tornadoes: an F2 in Renville County in 1997, an EF4 in Northwood in 2007, an EF3 in Ward County in 2010 and an EF2 in Watford City in 2018. Each of them resulted in one fatality.

> [Storm impact on North Dakota agriculture ‘tremendous,’ ag commissioner says](https://northdakotamonitor.com/2025/06/23/storm-impact-on-north-dakota-agriculture-tremendous-ag-commissioner-says/)

The deadliest North Dakota tornado on record took place June 20, 1957, in Fargo, an F5 that claimed 10 lives.

While the National Weather Service has yet to officially classify this weekend’s tornadoes, preliminary results suggest the storm that hit Enderlin was an EF3, according to Jacob Spender, a meteorologist for the agency’s Grand Forks Office.

The people who died in the Enderlin tornado late Friday were identified as Michael Dehn, 73, Katherine Pfaff-Dehn, 73, and Marcario Lucio, 89, according to the Cass County Sheriff’s Office.

A separate tornado that appeared south of Valley City has been preliminarily classified as a EF2, Spender said.

The Grand Forks office said Monday it has yet to determine how many tornadoes in total there were.

“We sent a flurry of different teams out to kind of assess the different damage across the area,” Spender said.

Gov. Kelly Armstrong is expected to tour the damage this week.

Episode NarrativeDuring the evening of Friday, June 20th into the early morning hours of June 21st, much of the region was affected by severe weather. Supercell thunderstorms developed across southeast North Dakota ahead of an approaching convective complex, producing multiple strong, destructive, and fatal tornadoes. This was followed by a powerful line of severe thunderstorms categorized as a derecho, which tracked across much of the region resulting in widespread straight line wind damage. After the derecho passed through the region, there was a period of prolonged destructive winds that affected portions of central and east central North Dakota, as well as adjacent portions of Minnesota. This was a unique event due to the combination of the violent tornadoes ahead of the derecho, and the long duration of significant winds that followed the derecho. Based on estimates provided by North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, the state lost anywhere from 50 to 80 million bushels of grain storage capacity from these storms.
Event NarrativeThis large and violent tornado began with minor damage to a few branches about 3 miles SSW Enderlin but within 2.5 miles of the track, the tornado gained intensity and significantly widened. While south of Highway 46, between 56th and 57th Street SE, the tornado derailed 33 train cars including 19 fully-loaded grain hopper cars and 14 empty tanker cars, mainly tipped from the track. Included in the derailed cars were one filled grain car (286,000 lbs) and four empty tanker cars (72,000 lbs) that were pulled into a field away from the track. One of the 4 tanker cars was tossed 600-1000 ft (183-305 m) from the track and an estimated 475.7 ft (145 m) from the distance of the previous tanker car it was attached to before being pulled off of the track; wheel sets detached near the point from which the cars were derailed from the track. It was in this train derailment location that EF-5 damage intensity was noted with greater than 210 mph winds listed officially for this tornado.
Extensive collaboration with wind damage experts provided forensic analyses for the train damage that occurred with this tornado. These analyses estimate potential wind speeds of approximately 230 mph are needed to completely overturn a fully loaded grain hopper car. Collaboration with the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University���s Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory estimated a potential wind speed of >119 m/s (>266 mph) to loft the empty tanker car 475.7 ft (145 m) using similar calculations performed in Estimating Wind Speeds in Tornadoes Using Debris Trajectories of Large Compact Objects (Miller et al. 2024). The study, published in the Monthly Weather Review, found that large compact objects lofted greater than 50 m indicate EF-5 intensity winds (greater than 200 mph). The Enderlin train cars were nearly 2�� farther than the EF-5 threshold distance and 4�� heavier than the heaviest object modeled in the study. The maximum wind speed also correlates to the timing of the maximum strength observed via the WSR-88D storm-relative velocity data from KMVX.
The tornado continued to widen as it tracked to the north and east. Just to the south of Highway 46, a free standing cell phone tower (FST DOD 2) collapsed, and it impacted several farmsteads with outbuildings destroyed. Extensive vegetation damage occurred with crops destroyed, bark stripped from trees with a ���sandpapering��� effect noted on numerous trees, and many large trees snapped or stubbed. Large tree root balls of 18-24��� diameter trunks were displaced, and in some cases, it was unknown where the uprooted trees originated from. EF-4 damage was noted with the trees. The tornado continued to track northward crossing Highway 46 into southwestern Cass County. The tornado statistics for the Ransom County portion include: a length of 5.4 miles, a maximum width of 1850 yards, a maximum wind of greater than 210 mph (EF-5), and 0 fatalities. Total track length between Ransom and Cass counties was 12.1 miles. Monetary damage estimates were not available.

North Dakota’s tornado changed EF rate
======================================

 

[Josephine Lau](https://theticker.org/staff_name/josephine-lau/), Copy Chief

December 8, 2025

 

[![Image 9: NWS Fort Worth I Wikimedia Commons](https://theticker.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/NWS-FORT-WORTH-I-WIKIMEDIA-COMMONS.jpg)](https://theticker.org/17689/science/2025-enderlin-tornado-upgraded-marking-u-s-s-first-ef5-in-12-years/#photo)

NWS Fort Worth I Wikimedia Commons

A tornado that touched down near Enderlin, N.D., on June 20, was [upgraded](https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf) to a rating EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, making it the first tornado since May 2013 to receive the rating.

The tornado, lasting 19 minutes with a 12-mile path, was part of a derecho — a widespread, long-lasting windstorm that accompanied several fast-moving thunderstorms or showers — that caused 41 tornadoes during the tornado outbreak from June 19 to June 22.

The tornado was initially rated EF3 by the National Weather Service in Grand Forks, N.D., but the rating was upgraded in October following a revised survey of the tornado’s damage.  
  
The revised survey was conducted by Tim Marshall, Jim LaDue, Connell Miller, Greg Kopp, David Sills and the Northern Tornadoes Project at the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory of Western University.

Most notably, the survey found that 33 derailed train cars weighing between 72,000 pounds and 286,000 pounds were thrown and landed nearly 500 feet from each other because of the tornado. Researchers and meteorologists found that “analyses estimate potential wind speeds of approximately 230 mph are needed to completely overturn a fully loaded grain hopper car,” [The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2025/10/11/north-dakota-tornado-ef5-rare-rating/) reports.

The [EF Scale](https://www.weather.gov/oun/efscale), operational since February 2007, is derived from the [Fujita Scale](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/fujita). Its estimated wind speed ranges are based on damage from the tornado. Ratings, which are given from levels zero to five, are assigned based on the highest wind speed that occurred on the tornado’s path.

The previous EF5 tornado prior to the “EF5 drought” in the U.S. was the 2013 Moore tornado, which occurred in Oklahoma.

The tornado caused three casualties and zero injuries. North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster on June 21 following the tornado. A month later, he made a request for a presidential disaster declaration for the damage dealt by the storms and tornados; the request was [approved](https://www.governor.nd.gov/news/president-trump-grants-armstrongs-request-major-disaster-declaration-severe-storm-damage-june) in September.

The approval would allow access to the Federal Emergency Management Agency funds.

“This much-needed disaster aid will help our state’s communities and utilities recover from one of the most powerful summer storms in recent history,” Armstrong said.

Days after the tornado, over 150 volunteers from different counties in the state [helped](https://www.agweek.com/weather/we-all-come-together-over-150-volunteers-clean-up-enderlin-farms-after-deadly-tornadoes) clean debris from farm fields in Enderlin. Drones were also used to search for missing belongings from damaged houses.

The town will continue rebuilding in the months following the tornado. In fact, mental health services and funds, such as the [Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund](https://www.wdayradionow.com/news/local-news/local-bank-sets-up-fund-for-enderlin-tornado-victims/) Relief Fund from BankNorth, have been set up for families affected by the storms, including the tornado.

Still, “people don’t realize what it costs to rebuild or they thought their insurance had something, but then they realize it wasn’t what they thought it said it was,” Maggie Peters from the Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund [said](https://www.inforum.com/news/north-dakota/fargo-fashion-show-set-to-help-enderlin-tornado-victims).
